title: M17, Omega
caption: The Omega Nebula (M17), imaged by the WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope
credit: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage) and WIYN

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: This wide view shows M17 in Sagittarius, a nebula with many informal names, among them the Omega, the Swan and the Lobster Nebula. It ranks among the biggest and brightest regions of star formation in our galaxy.

Being so large and bright, M17 was one of the earliest nebulae ever found, discovered back in 1745. Its hydrogen gas glows with a distinctive red color, energized by hot, massive blue stars buried within the cloud.

Nebulae like this are stellar nurseries. When young, massive stars switch on, their intense ultraviolet light strips electrons from the surrounding hydrogen atoms. As the atoms recapture those electrons, they give off light at particular colors, which is why such clouds glow. The same stars also carve and sculpt the gas around them, shaping the nebula as it evolves.

understand.summary: The WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used three narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in orange, oxygen [O III] in green and sulfur [S II] in blue.
